title: Burst recovery and fairness heuristics field notes
content:
Summary:

Field notes from exploratory tuning runs around continuous-batcher behavior under short, high-intensity microbursts. Focus is on recovery speed (how quickly latency and throughput return to steady-state after a burst), fairness across priority classes during overload, and the trade-offs introduced by various eviction/flush heuristics. This doc captures setups, raw observations, profiler outputs, and proposed short-term mitigations.

Motivation / problem statement:
- We see recurring 10–100ms microbursts that create long tail spikes (p99 > 300ms) even when p50/p95 look healthy.
- Root cause is often batch formation + a small number of long-wait requests creating head-of-line blocking.
- Need a scheduler policy that:
  1) recovers throughput rapidly after a burst,
  2) prevents a small noisy group from causing long tails for other traffic,
  3) preserves fairness (SLOs for paid tiers) without causing throughput collapse.

Experiment scope and constraints:
- Hardware: 1x A100 80GB per pod, 4 pods per node in test cluster (k8s ephemeral cluster), same kernel/driver baseline as prod-rls-2025-01.
- Model: mix of Llama2-13B (quantized) and smaller 7B eval variant to mimic heterogeneous inference mix.
- Traffic shapes: steady low (2 rps/pod), bursty short (200 reqs in 200ms), medium burst (1k reqs over 2s), prioritized classes (tier-high, tier-standard).
- Duration: individual runs 10–15 minutes; repeated 6 times per config.
- Observed metrics: p50/p90/p95/p99 latency, mean batch size, batch size distribution histogram, queue depth over time, eviction events, CPU/GPU utilization, kernel stall %, scheduler wakeups/sec.

Profiling summary (high level):
- CPU: scheduler thread occasionally spikes context-switches during aggressive eviction runs. Syscall blocking observed when we call into NVML for GPU mem checks (introduces ~0.5-1ms jitter).
- GPU: utilization dips during burst recovery as tiny batches flood the device; kernel dispatch overhead becomes dominant.
- Runtime internals: KV cache warmup/misses amplify first-req latency when eviction churn is high.
- I/O: no significant networking saturation in these runs; bottlenecks are internal batching and dispatch.

Key hypotheses going into tuning runs:
1) Small flush timeouts reduce p99 when arrival variability is small, but harm throughput and increase cost under sustained load.
2) Age-aware eviction (prefer evicting oldest low-priority in-batch candidates) helps tail latency without hurting high-priority SLOs.
3) Adding a short "burst drain" mode (temporarily raise max batch size and reduce timeout) recovers throughput faster but needs careful fairness clamps.

Tuning knobs tested (explicit):
- flush_timeout_ms: 3, 8, 15, 30
- max_batch_size: 8, 16, 32, 64
- fairness_weight: priority scaling factor for admission (0.5, 1, 2 for standard->high mapping)
- age_eviction_threshold_ms: 40, 120
- burst_mode_trigger_qps: threshold of queued requests (40, 80) to enable aggressive coalescing
- eviction_policy: oldest-first vs size-first vs priority-aware

Representative runs and observations:
1) Config A (flush=8ms, max_batch=32, no age-eviction):
   - Steady-state: p50 12ms, p95 48ms, p99 210ms.
   - On burst: p99 spikes to ~420ms and takes ~9s to return to baseline; mean batch size drops to 6 during burst.
   - Notes: throughput maintained, but tail hurt by head-of-line long-waits from a few large context requests.

2) Config B (flush=3ms, max_batch=16, age-eviction=120ms):
   - Steady-state: p50 14ms, p95 60ms, p99 180ms.
   - On burst: p99 peaks lower (~310ms) and recovers in ~4s.
   - Side effect: overall throughput reduced ~6% under sustained high input due to smaller batch cap.

3) Config C (burst_mode_trigger=40, burst_mode: max_batch=64, flush=15ms, priority clamps enabled):
   - Steady-state: p50 13ms, p95 50ms, p99 200ms.
   - On burst: initial p99 high (~380ms) but recovery <3s; batch sizes temporarily spiked to 48 and device utilization improved.
   - Fairness: without clamps, standard-tier p99 regresses by ~25%. With clamps (priority share floor), high-tier maintained but standard-tier saw slight increase in p95.

4) Config D (age_eviction=40ms, eviction_policy=priority-aware):
   - Observed best mixed outcome for tail distribution across tiers. p99 for standard-tier down 30% vs baseline during bursts; high-tier unchanged.
   - However scheduler thread CPU spikes increased; additional tuning needed to avoid excess polling.

Profiler traces (notes):
- Flame samples point to increased time in batch_coalesce() when eviction policy checks priority metadata — we added a hashmap look-up per candidate; this is a hot path.
- System trace shows a correlation between NVML GPU mem queries and scheduler wake latency; batching thread waits on synchronous GPU checks in our health probe.
- Kernel dispatch shows many short-lived kernels when batch sizes are small; overall GPU efficiency suffers.

Bottlenecks identified:
- Metadata lookup cost in hot path when applying priority-aware eviction. We can micro-opt: inline a fast-path for common-case (no-priority) and use lock-free ring buffers for per-priority counts.
- Synchronous NVML checks in scheduler health checks: should make these async or cached for 200ms windows to avoid adding ~1ms jitter on each decision.
- KV-cache churn: eviction of items while multiple requests in flight causes cache misses and rehydration costs — possible mitigation: protect active requests from eviction for one batch cycle.

Design proposals and trade-offs:
1) Age-aware priority eviction: evict oldest standard-tier candidates first once they exceed X ms wait OR when queue depth crosses Y. Pro: reduces long tails for others. Con: additional CPU on hot path; must be implemented with O(1) checks.

2) Burst drain mode with fairness clamps: upon detecting a microburst (queue > threshold for T ms), enable temporary larger max_batch and short timeout but apply per-priority tokens so high-tier only gets e.g. 40% of extra slots. Pro: faster device utilization and shorter recovery. Con: complexity; risk of starving standard-tier if clamps wrong.

3) Async GPU health telemetry: move NVML queries off the scheduler-critical thread; use sampled/cached values to decide bulk eviction.

Quick wins (low engineering cost):
- Change NVML call to cached async with 200ms TTL. Test for removal of 1ms jitter.
- Implement fast-path for no-priority requests to skip hashmap lookup.
- Protect in-flight requests from eviction for a single flush cycle (cheap flag).

Next experiments to run (concrete):
- Run Config C with priority clamps tuned at 30/50/70% share for high-tier and measure 6-hour run for steady-state cost impact.
- Implement cached NVML and re-run Config D to see if CPU spikes persist.
- Microbench the hashmap lookup vs inline array for common-case to quantify overheads (target <100ns per decision).

Runbook changes (proposed):
- Add an emergency flag "burst_recovery_mode" toggle in runtime to quickly enable larger max_batch and fairness clamps from operator UI.
- Dashboard: add a "burst events" panel (burst start/stop, queue depth heatmap, recovery latency over 60s) and alert when >3 events/hour.

Open questions / unresolved:
- What is acceptable throughput loss in exchange for improved p99 under bursts? Product needs to weigh cost vs SLA.
- Should we bias eviction toward long-running-context requests even if they are high-priority? (likely not)
- Is KV-cache eviction policy adjustable per-priority? Could we pin small working sets for paid tiers?

Action items (owners):
- Aisha: prototype NVML async cache & flag for protecting in-flight requests (due 2025-03-05).
- Jason: implement fast-path priority lookup (PR stubbed, see linked PR) and microbench (due 2025-03-08).
- María: dashboard panels + alert thresholds (due 2025-03-04).
- Rahil: run long-duration Config C cost/run analysis and produce cost-versus-p99 summary (due 2025-03-12).

Notes to reviewers:
- This is an exploratory doc; code changes should prioritize safety — burst_recovery_mode should be operator-only until we validate 72h of runs.
- Avoid adding blocking syscalls on the scheduler hot path. Any health checks should be offloaded.

Appendix: quick raw numbers (run sample averages across 6 repeats):
- Baseline: p99 210ms, recovery time 9.1s, avg batch size during burst 6.1, GPU duty-cycle drop 22%.
- Best observed: p99 160ms, recovery 2.8s, avg batch size 42 during burst when burst_mode enabled, cost +4.8% on token compute for the trial window.

End of notes.
